findings.issue: States 'Use à le for masculine places, such as au marché.' The form à le never occurs in French; à + le obligatorily contracts to au. Teaches a nonexistent form.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite: 'À + la stays à la (à la boulangerie). À + le contracts to au: au marché, au café.'

findings.issue: Claims 'In Québec, the same ideas are expressed with the same words.' Québec counters commonly use pour ici ou pour emporter; sur place is far less usual there. Regional claim is inaccurate.
findings.suggestion: Replace with: 'In France: sur place ou à emporter. In Québec you will usually hear pour ici ou pour emporter.' Align words[7].noteEnglish (pour emporter) with this Québec note.

findings.issue: Spanish source 'natural' = freshly squeezed. In French café usage that is jus d'orange pressé; frais reads as chilled or not stale. The draft's own term note and teachingNotesEnglish[6] say pressé is the menu word, so phrase, speaking line and reading line contradict the notes.
findings.suggestion: Use 'Vous avez du jus d'orange pressé ?' in all three places, and add to the note: 'frais means chilled or not stale; pressé means freshly squeezed.'

findings.issue: 'ask for les toilettes or la salle de bain at a hotel' invites a false friend: salle de bain is the bathroom with a shower, not the toilet. A learner asking a café for la salle de bain will not be understood.
findings.suggestion: Drop salle de bain or state: 'Ask for les toilettes. La salle de bain is a hotel-room bathroom with a shower, never the café toilet.'

findings.field: words[4].noteEnglish, words[12].fr, speakingFrench, passage.french[4] (sur la terrasse)
findings.issue: Sur la terrasse is grammatical but the fixed café idiom is en terrasse (s'asseoir / s'installer en terrasse).
findings.suggestion: Use 'Est-ce que je peux m'asseoir en terrasse ?' and note 'en terrasse is the café idiom'; keep sur la terrasse only as a literal gloss.

findings.field: words[14].fr (Vous faites des œufs à la demande ?)
findings.issue: À la demande means on request, not cooked to taste. For huevos al gusto the café wording is œufs au choix or comme vous voulez.
findings.suggestion: 'Vous faites les œufs au choix ?' with note 'au choix = cooked the way you ask; comme vous voulez is also heard.'

findings.issue: 'le pain grillé vient avec du beurre' calques English 'comes with'; venir avec is not idiomatic for a dish.
findings.suggestion: 'Oui, le pain grillé est servi avec du beurre et de la confiture.'

findings.issue: English anchor is 'is going to go'. Draft uses present va à, dropping the lesson's target structure; the authoring note calls va aller awkward, but Emma va aller à la boulangerie is normal French.
findings.suggestion: 'Ensuite, Emma va aller à la boulangerie chercher du pain.' and correct the authoring note.

findings.issue: 'Diego le barista fait le café' uses English apposition order and fait for brewing.
findings.suggestion: 'Au comptoir, le barista Diego prépare le café.'

findings.issue: Focus lists avoir envie de + infinitif but no word, phrase, speaking line or reading line uses it; it appears only in teachingNotesEnglish[3].
findings.suggestion: Either add one learner item (e.g. 'J'ai envie d'un café.') or remove avoir envie de from both focus fields.

findings.issue: Focus names regular -ir verbs (choisir) but no learner item uses one; only teachingNotesEnglish[1] does.
findings.suggestion: Add a phrase such as 'Je choisis les œufs brouillés.' or drop choisir from the focus.

findings.issue: Note says vous is for someone you have just met; passage and speaking line use tu with Lucía, whom Emma has just met. Inherited from the Spanish source, but the French note contradicts the reading.
findings.suggestion: Change the note to: 'Vous is the safe form with staff or a stranger; between hotel guests of the same age, tu is common, as in the reading.'

findings.issue: Bare haricots in a French food context often suggests haricots verts; Mexican frijoles are haricots rouges or haricots noirs.
findings.suggestion: Add to note: 'For Mexican-style beans say haricots noirs or haricots rouges; haricots verts are green beans.'

findings.issue: 'Les WC is more informal' is imprecise; WC is neutral and widely used on signs and in speech.
findings.suggestion: 'Les toilettes is the everyday word; les WC also appears on signs and is equally acceptable.'

findings.issue: The note says 'Use à le for masculine places, such as au marché.' This is a grammar error shown to learners: à + le always contracts to au, and 'à le' is never correct. The contractions au and du also appear in the passage without explanation (au comptoir, au fond, près du marché).
findings.suggestion: Replace with: 'With a masculine place, à + le becomes au: Je vais au marché. De + le becomes du: près du marché. À la and à l’ do not change.' Add the same rule to teachingNotesEnglish[0].

findings.field: teachingNotesEnglish[5]; words['Do you drink coffee or tea?'].noteEnglish; passage.french lines 5 and 7; speakingFrench
findings.issue: This copies the Spanish tú rule ('tu with a fellow guest your age'). In French, vous is the default with an adult you have just met, and Lucía is a parent at a hotel. The lesson is also inconsistent: the phrase list teaches 'Vous habitez ici ?' as polite for someone you just met, but the passage and speakingFrench use 'Tu habites ici ?' with that same person. Lesson 4 teachingNotesEnglish[7] repeats the same rule.
findings.suggestion: Reword the note: 'Use vous with adults you have just met. Switch to tu when the other person uses it or suggests it (On peut se tutoyer ?). Young travellers often use tu with each other.' Either add a passage line where Lucía says 'On peut se tutoyer ?' before Emma's tu questions, or change speakingFrench to '… Vous buvez du café ou du thé ? Vous habitez ici ?' Apply the same fix to the Lesson 4 note.

findings.field: words['Do you make eggs to order?'].fr and .noteEnglish
findings.issue: 'Vous faites des œufs à la demande ?' is not how French speakers say eggs cooked the way you like. 'À la demande' means 'on request'. 'Au choix' means 'your choice of' an item, not how it is cooked. The authoring note calls both options natural.
findings.suggestion: Use 'Vous faites les œufs comme je veux ?' (or '… à mon goût ?'). Note: 'Faire means to make or do. Comme je veux means the way I want: brouillés, au plat…'

findings.issue: 'Emma va à la boulangerie chercher du pain' drops the aller + infinitive form for the source line 'is going to go'. The note gives a wrong reason: 'va aller' is standard French and is a good example of this lesson's focus.
findings.suggestion: 'Ensuite, Emma va aller à la boulangerie chercher du pain.' Delete the 'awkward aller + aller' claim from the authoring note.

findings.field: words['Can I sit on the terrace?'].fr; words['the terrace'].noteEnglish; passage.french line 5; speakingFrench
findings.issue: French cafés say 's’asseoir en terrasse'. 'Sur la terrasse' is understood but less natural.
findings.suggestion: 'Est-ce que je peux m’asseoir en terrasse ?' Note: 'En terrasse means outside at a café’s tables.'

findings.issue: 'In Oaxaca, the restroom is often at the back of the café' is an unsupported generalization. 'Ask for la salle de bain at a hotel' is wrong for France, where it means a room with a bath or shower. In Québec, 'la salle de bain' is a common way to ask for the restroom.
findings.suggestion: 'Ask Où sont les toilettes ? In Québec, la salle de bain is also common.' Delete the Oaxaca generalization. In the restroom word note, change 'WC is more informal' to 'WC is common on signs.'

findings.issue: 'In Québec, the same ideas are expressed with the same words' contradicts the word note. Québec usually says 'pour emporter', and France says 'à emporter'.
findings.suggestion: 'France: sur place / à emporter. Québec: pour emporter is usual, and pour manger ici is also heard.'

findings.issue: 'Le pain grillé vient avec du beurre' copies English 'comes with'.
findings.suggestion: 'Oui, le pain grillé est servi avec du beurre et de la confiture.'

findings.field: words['Do you have fresh orange juice?'].fr; passage.french line 2; speakingFrench
findings.issue: 'Jus d’orange frais' can mean chilled juice. The source means freshly squeezed, and the draft's own term note says pressé.
findings.suggestion: 'Vous avez du jus d’orange pressé ?' Keep frais only in 'des fruits frais'.

findings.issue: Avoir envie de is in the focus, but no phrase, passage line or speaking task practises it. The focus says '+ infinitif', yet the note's example uses a noun (d’un thé). The partitive (du, de la, des) is explained in a word note and used throughout, but it is not in the focus.
findings.suggestion: Add a phrase such as 'J’ai envie d’un café.' or 'J’ai envie de manger des fruits.' Change the focus to 'avoir envie de + nom/infinitif'. Add the partitive du/de la/des to focusEnglish.

findings.issue: There is no Québec regional note, though Lessons 1–3 give regional notes for breakfast vocabulary.
findings.suggestion: Append: 'In Québec, toast is usually des rôties.'

findings.issue: Choisir (regular -ir) is in the focus, but no word, passage line or speaking task uses it.
findings.suggestion: Add a phrase such as 'Je choisis les chilaquiles.' or 'Vous choisissez quoi ?', or remove choisir from the focus.

findings.issue: Beginners are not told the most important present-tense sound rule: the -ent ending of ils/elles is silent, so mangent sounds like mange.
findings.suggestion: Add: 'The -ent of ils mangent / ils boivent is silent: je mange, tu manges, il mange and ils mangent sound the same.'

findings.issue: 'Jambon is cooked ham' is inaccurate, because jambon cru (cured ham) is also jambon. 'Yolk uncooked' should say runny.
findings.suggestion: 'Jambon is ham. Jambon blanc is cooked, jambon cru is cured.' For the eggs: 'usually with a runny yolk'.

findings.issue: 'The usual word for beans in a café' is odd in a Mexico scene. French usually calls Mexican-style beans haricots noirs or haricots rouges.
findings.suggestion: 'Beans are les haricots. Mexican beans are often haricots noirs, and menus may keep the Spanish word frijoles.'

minorRemaining: Lesson 5 words[14].fr 'Vous pouvez faire les œufs comme je les aime ?' is grammatical and comprehensible, but a server cannot know how you like them; more natural café wording is 'Vous pouvez faire les œufs comme je veux ?' or 'Je peux choisir la cuisson des œufs ?'. Correctly flagged as a native-review gate in authoringNotesEnglish[1].

Lesson 6 learner items use vous only (words[11], words[12], speakingFrench, passage); the source lesson deliberately contrasts tú (fellow guest) with usted (someone just met). The French register is self-consistent and defensible, but the tu form now appears only in teachingNotesEnglish[0]; consider one tu item (e.g. 'Tu bois du café ou du thé ?' with a fellow-guest note) so the lesson still teaches the contrast.

Lesson 6 words[7].fr 'la salsa verte' mixes the Spanish loan with a French adjective; French menus write 'salsa verde' or 'sauce verte (mexicaine)'. Note's claim that 'sauce verte' is an alternative is loose: in France 'sauce verte' usually means an herb sauce. Suggest 'la salsa verde' with note 'a Spanish loan kept as is in French'.
Lesson 4 teachingNotesEnglish[2] 'un or une becomes d'un or d'une' is imprecise: it is de + un/une that elides to d'un/d'une. Suggest 'de + une becomes d'une: j'ai besoin d'une serviette.'
Lesson 6 passage.french[0] 'pour le petit-déjeuner' is acceptable; 'au petit-déjeuner' is the more idiomatic choice and matches speakingFrench.

Lesson 6 words[15] note calls ouvrir 'irregular' while teachingNotesEnglish[3] says it follows the -er pattern in the present; both are true but the two labels may confuse a beginner. Suggest 'Ouvrir ends in -ir but takes -er endings in the present'.
